title: Extra Watchers Will Be on Duty at Polling Places on Election Day
summary:
When Americans vote in the midterm elections on November 3, extra watchers will be on duty at many polling places. The U.S. Department of Justice, or DOJ, plans to send about 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states. That is more than double the number used in the 2022 midterms.

Monitors have a quiet job. They stand back, watch how voting is run, and report what they see. Their purpose is to make sure voting-rights laws are followed, so nobody is wrongly turned away or scared off from voting. “They're there to just do as their name suggests, which is to observe,” said Stacey Young, a former DOJ lawyer who has been a monitor three times. Monitors never run the voting, and the department says they have been told clearly not to interfere.

Why are some state officials worried this year? The effort is much bigger than usual. David Becker, a former DOJ voting-rights attorney, called the scale “not normal,” but said he is “not particularly concerned.” Also, prosecutors will be allowed to serve as monitors this year, something long-standing rules did not allow. A senior DOJ official said monitors will focus on busy areas and places that have had problems with language or disability access.

The monitors will visit only Election Day polling places, not early-voting sites.
why_it_matters: Fair voting rules protect everyone's voice in an election, including the grown-ups who vote on things that shape your school and neighborhood.
